pitchHistory.title: The Minecraft Movie Wasn't Supposed to Work — So Why Did It Break the Internet?
pitchHistory.summary: The Minecraft movie adaptation arrived with all the energy of a corporate PowerPoint and somehow became the most culturally alive thing to happen to cinema in years — not despite its absurdity, but because of it. This post unpacks why the film's chaotic audience response (the screaming, the throwing, the unhinged theatrical rituals) is less about the movie itself and more about a generation that grew up inside a game and finally got to perform that identity in public. It's a story about nostalgia as a social technology, and why the internet didn't just watch the Minecraft movie — it became part of it.

pitchHistory.title: RIP Memes (2009–2025): Why the Internet Is Trying to Reboot Itself Back to 2016
pitchHistory.summary: The 'Great Meme Reset' — a viral movement demanding internet culture revert to pre-brainrot, pre-AI 2016 memes — sounds like a joke, but it's actually a genuine symptom of something worth taking seriously: the industrialisation of humour. When memes have a 48-hour shelf life, when AI slops out ten thousand 'Italian Brainrot' creatures before breakfast, and when every brand is in your comments doing the bit, what does it mean that people are nostalgically reaching for Trollface like it's a lost golden age? This post unpacks what the Meme Reset reveals about authenticity, algorithmic anxiety, and why the internet keeps trying to escape itself.

pitchHistory.title: The Vampires Were Always the Music Industry: How 'Sinners' Became the Horror Film That Ate Hollywood
pitchHistory.summary: Ryan Coogler's 1930s Mississippi vampire epic just won 4 Oscars, broke records with 16 nominations, and grossed nearly $400 million — but the real story is what's hiding inside the genre clothes: a full-throated argument about who gets to own Black music, told through blues guitar and bloodsuckers. This post unpacks why 'Sinners' isn't just a great horror film but a cultural thesis statement arriving at exactly the right moment, and what it means that Hollywood's most self-congratulatory night finally had to reckon with it.

pitchHistory.title: YouTube Ate Hollywood and Nobody Noticed: The Sidemen, MrBeast, and the Creator-to-Netflix Pipeline That's Rewriting the Rules of Fame
pitchHistory.summary: The Sidemen's 'Inside' just dropped on Netflix, MrBeast has been colonising streaming for years, and the old line between 'influencer' and 'prestige content' has quietly dissolved — so what does it mean when the people who built their empires by being parasocially accessible to millions are now playing by Hollywood's rules? This post digs into the creator economy's hostile takeover of traditional entertainment, why Netflix keeps writing cheques to YouTubers, and what it reveals about how attention, loyalty, and stardom have been fundamentally rewired in the algorithmic age.

pitchHistory.title: Valerie Cherish Saw It Coming: How 'The Comeback' Became the Most Accidentally Prophetic Show on Television
pitchHistory.summary: HBO's 'The Comeback' returned after 11+ years with Lisa Kudrow's Valerie Cherish starring in Hollywood's first AI-written sitcom — a premise so perfectly timed it landed the same week the WGA signed a new contract specifically to limit AI in writers' rooms. This post argues that 'The Comeback' has now done it three times: debuted in 2005 mocking reality TV before reality TV ate everything, returned in 2014 to skewer streaming prestige culture right as it peaked, and come back in 2026 as a brutal comedy about AI displacement — except this time, the satire isn't ahead of the curve, it *is* the curve. It's the rare show that doesn't just reflect the culture; it keeps arriving at exactly the right moment to tell us what we're too uncomfortable to say straight.
